title: The Pardoner's Tale
text:
In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, the Pardoner told of three young rioters drinking in a tavern in Flanders early one morning during a time of plague. They heard a bell as a corpse was carried past and learned that it was an old friend of theirs, killed in the night by a thief called Death, who had slain a thousand people in the area.

Drunk and furious, the three swore an oath to be brothers to one another and to find and kill Death. On the road they met a poor old man and roughly demanded to know where Death was. He told them that they would find him under an oak tree at the end of a crooked path.

Under the tree they found a heap of gold coins. They forgot all about Death. They decided to wait until night to carry the gold away safely, and they drew lots to send one to town for bread and wine. The youngest went.

While he was gone, the other two agreed to kill him when he returned and split the gold two ways. Meanwhile, the youngest bought poison and put it into two of the three bottles of wine, so that he could keep the gold for himself. When he came back, the two stabbed him. Then they sat down and drank the wine. And so all three found Death under the tree.
lesson: A group bound only by greed has no real loyalty, and each member is a threat to the others the moment there is something to divide. Build partnerships on more than shared gain.
location: England (tale set in Flanders, modern Belgium)
source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Pardoner's Tale
